children: Microfinance is one of India’s deepest financial-inclusion networks, serving about 6.27 crore active borrowers across 685 districts. These households often depend on agriculture, livestock, vending, informal work and small businesses, making them particularly exposed to floods, heatwaves, droughts and erratic rainfall.

The Economic Survey 2025-26 records NBFC-MFIs with 39 per cent of microfinance loan outstanding, followed by banks at 32 per cent, small finance banks at 16 per cent and other NBFCs at 12 per cent. While conventional asset-quality risks are closely monitored, climate-related credit risk remains less visible.

Microfinance lenders track days past due, portfolio at risk, collection efficiency, and NPAs. These indicators show what happened to a loan, but not necessarily why. A borrower may become delinquent because of over-borrowing — or because a flood destroyed a crop, extreme heat prevented outdoor work or a cyclone disrupted local commerce.

Evidence already points to this connection. MFIN has reported heatwaves affecting borrower livelihoods and repayment ability. Bandhan Bank has linked Assam floods to weaker collections and slippages, while rating agencies have highlighted natural calamities as risks to repayment and collection efficiency.

A World Bank analysis of Northern Arc Capital’s portfolios provides stronger evidence. Across 27,000 microfinance loans in nine districts during the 2018 Kerala floods, collection efficiency fell from 96 per cent to 60 per cent during the flood month. After Cyclone Fani, analysis of 75,000 loans across 14 districts found collection efficiency declining from 97 per cent to 90 per cent before recovering. Yet India lacks a standard public dataset showing what proportion of microfinance delinquency is attributable to verified climate events.

The treatment exists, but is at best fragmented. For instance, The Credit Guarantee Scheme for Microfinance Institutions 2.0 facilitates up to ₹20,000 crore of credit and was estimated to benefit around 36 lakh borrowers. However, it primarily addresses funding stress rather than identifying climate-affected portfolios.

The RBI’s natural-calamity framework permits restructuring and fresh lending to affected borrowers. Meanwhile, MFIN, with ADB support, is developing a parametric natural-catastrophe insurance initiative.
Three steps can help bridge the gap between climate risk and microfinance risk.

First, capture the cause alongside delinquency. When repayment deteriorates after a verified flood, drought, cyclone or heatwave, lenders should tag the event against geography, livelihood and subsequent repayment performance. Pakistan’s World Bank-backed Resilient and Accessible Microfinance Project offers a useful example through its Climate Risk Facility.

Second, make climate information part of credit-risk assessment. MFIs can combine district-level hazard data with borrower livelihoods and branch concentration. A dairy borrower in a drought-prone district and a trader in a flood-prone market face different risks even when conventional credit indicators appear similar.

Third, pre-design relief mechanisms. Temporary disruption may require repayment flexibility or emergency liquidity, while persistent livelihood damage may require restructuring, insurance or adaptation finance. Research on BRAC’s pre-approved emergency loans for flood-exposed borrowers found benefits for household resilience alongside improved repayment and branch profitability.

India has microfinance support schemes, disaster-relief provisions and emerging climate-risk tools, but these remain disconnected. Linking physical events to livelihood losses, repayment deterioration and appropriate relief can turn climate risk from an episodic disruption into a measurable credit-risk factor — enabling lenders to move from generic relief towards targeted and longer-term solutions.
Jindal is a Senior Economist, and Rai is Vice President, at a private Indian bank.

title: India’s microfinance sector must prepare for rising climate risks
